title: A Soviet Spy's Embarrassing Secret Nearly Stopped World War III
dek: In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked into MI6 and offered to spy for the West — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.
why: Ben Macintyre tells a Cold War spy story that has never been told before, with astonishing detail and tight pacing — though the information density is concentrated in the second half, on the coup and its aftermath, while the setup runs a little long.
who: Listeners interested in Cold War spy history, the Iranian Revolution and intelligence operations; readers who like Ben Macintyre's narrative style; anyone who wants to understand how intelligence work accidentally shaped the modern Middle East.
skip: The sponsor read at the top and the promo at the end can be skipped; the episode proper starts at 3:01.

points.h: A spy story that has never been told
points.body: Ben Macintyre's new book Redwood tells a Cold War story that had never been made public before: in 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran, Vladimir Kuzichkin, walked into MI6 and offered to become a double agent codenamed "Redwood." The intelligence he provided revealed that the Soviets were plotting a coup through the Iranian communist Tudeh Party to overthrow Khomeini's government, after which the Red Army would cross into Iran from Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. The Pentagon's answer to that was nuclear strikes — because conventional forces were not enough to stop a full Soviet invasion. What makes the story so strange is that Kuzichkin's motive for defecting was intensely personal: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed Western medicine could cure him.

points.h: 1981 came closer to nuclear war than the Cuban Missile Crisis
points.body: Ben Macintyre points out that 1981 was one of the closest moments of nuclear confrontation in the Cold War, second only to the Cuban Missile Crisis. After the Iranian Revolution, every faction — nationalists, liberals, communists and Islamists — was fighting for power, and Tehran became a "seething cauldron of spies." The CIA, MI6 and the KGB all poured in at once. The Soviets had just invaded Afghanistan and were making good progress, while the Americans were desperate to re-establish a foothold in the Middle East. If the Soviets took Iran, they could control warm-water ports and oil fields and win the Cold War. So the Pentagon was already drawing up nuclear options, including using portable nuclear weapons to blow up mountain ranges and block Soviet armored columns.

points.h: The CIA was blind in Tehran; MI6 broke the rules and kept a man there
points.body: After the Iran hostage crisis, the CIA was thrown out of Tehran, had no human intelligence in Iran at all, and knew nothing about a possible Soviet coup. The only service still capable of operating was MI6, but Britain's condition for maintaining a diplomatic mission in 1981 was that it conduct "no spying whatsoever." MI6 nevertheless sent Ian McCready in under commercial counselor cover — a huge gamble by the British government. McCready's instructions were "do nothing, recruit no one, keep a low profile" — because if he was caught, the Iranians would take the entire embassy hostage. He could only communicate with London using a Second World War-era cipher machine called RockX, an extremely cumbersome device of which only two existed in the world.

points.h: His motive was impotence, not money or ideology
points.body: Kuzichkin was a senior officer at the KGB residency in Tehran, ran illegal spy programs across the entire Middle East, and was the only defector who understood how the illegal system worked. He walked into MI6 on his own and offered to spy for the West. The spy world has an acronym, MICE — money, ideology, coercion, ego — but Kuzichkin fit none of the categories. He was partly alienated from the regime, but the root cause was this: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed the West had a drug that could cure it. He had just married, loved his wife deeply, and could not reveal the secret to his KGB colleagues or to Soviet doctors. McCready did not mock him or exploit him; he took him with extreme seriousness, and even sent MI6 headquarters an unprecedented telex: "Help. What do I do with a spy who has erectile dysfunction?"

points.h: He photographed every KGB file in the Middle East
points.body: For nearly a year, McCready ran Kuzichkin by old-fashioned tradecraft: dead drops, brush contacts, miniature cameras. He gave Kuzichkin a Minox miniature camera to carry into the office every day and photograph every document he could get his hands on. In the end the Redwood archive filled four truckloads. MI6 gave him the codename "Redwood" — because he was six foot four, and because they could not resist the pun: Red for communism, Wood for his "problem." Kuzichkin's core intelligence was this: the Soviets were plotting a coup through the Tudeh Party, the money and weapons were already in place, the Tudeh had a secret military underground, and Kuzichkin himself was the coordinator between the KGB and the Tudeh Party.

points.h: The US and Britain handed the coup plan to the Iranians
points.body: After Kuzichkin fled to Britain, MI6 debated internally whether to use the intelligence. Chris Curnow, who ran the operations department and later became chief of MI6, argued it had to be used. He said that if they did not use it, intelligence about a communist Tudeh coup was meaningless. So MI6 sent Redwood to Islamabad, Pakistan, under diplomatic cover, to meet Iranian intelligence. The meeting lasted three days, Kuzichkin laid everything out, and MI6 handed the Iranians all four truckloads of intelligence. It was also an attempt to open a secret channel to Iran at a time when Tehran's relations with the West were dire. It was deeply illegal, and if it had come out it would have been a huge scandal — the British and American governments acting to protect the Islamic Revolution.

points.h: Iran used the intelligence to execute eight thousand communists
points.body: Once the Revolutionary Guard had the intelligence, it arrested eight thousand Iranian communists within two months, and about half of them were executed. This became a cornerstone of Iran's modern theocratic state. From that moment on, Khomeini tolerated no opposition at all; everyone was purged, including people already in prison, and it turned into a massacre. It also reinforced two convictions of the Islamic Revolution: first, that all opposition must be destroyed, because fifth columns were everywhere; second, that whatever happens, the British are behind it. MI6 and the CIA inadvertently consolidated the Iranian regime and created a monster — almost an exact replay of Afghanistan, where money poured in to Islamic guerrillas fighting the Soviets and ultimately produced al-Qaeda, ISIS and 9/11.

points.h: History is often driven by perception, not fact
points.body: Ben Macintyre stresses that it is impossible to know whether the Soviets would actually have carried out the coup, but everyone involved believed they would. McCready believed it, Kuzichkin believed it, and MI6, the CIA, the KGB and the Tudeh Party itself all believed it. That was enough — nuclear war can break out on the basis of perception rather than fact, and the same was true of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Would Khrushchev really have used those weapons? We do not know, but everyone believed he might. The story was never told because none of the participants wanted it told: not the Iranians, because it meant the West had outsmarted them again; not the KGB, because it was a humiliation — they had failed to spot the defector, 18 Soviet diplomats were expelled from Iran as a result, the entire Tudeh Party operation was dismantled, and agent networks across the Middle East and even in Canada were exposed.
